asking.answers: Each question comes with two to four short answers to tap, plus “Something else” and “Just draw it”.
asking.brief: Once it has enough, the clarifier writes a brief, usually a sentence or two, and picks a style: photography, illustration, minimal or 3D render. From there the drawing steps only see the brief, never the conversation.
asking.cap: The agent gets three questions per picture, and I enforce that in code instead of trusting the model with it. If the model tries a fourth, I ignore it and draw with what we have.
asking.enough: Before drawing, a clarifier model checks whether it has enough to go on. My rule for enough is a subject, a style, and at least one of setting, lighting or framing. If something is missing, it asks about one thing at a time, in that order.
asking.title: Asking before drawing

drawing.first_reviewer: My first reviewer failed on every image, and the fallback saved each failure as a pass with made-up scores. That was worse than having no review. Now, if no reviewer can be reached, the picture goes out with no score and a note saying it wasn’t checked.
drawing.order: My first version, in Python, let the model pick which tool to call next. Its prompt spelled out the order anyway, and tool calling didn’t fit steps that can switch provider halfway through. So here the order is code:
drawing.prompt: The prompt writer is asked for 60 to 120 words describing only what should be in the picture. Telling an image model what to leave out tends to put it in.
drawing.review: The reviewer is a vision model. It scores relevance, quality, style match and composition out of 10, plus an overall score and suggestions. A picture passes with 7 overall and at least 6 for relevance. I keep the better of the two attempts.
drawing.step_rewrite: If the review fails, rewrite the prompt with up to three of the reviewer’s notes
drawing.step_write: Write an image prompt from the brief
drawing.storage: Pictures go into a storage bucket, named with a hash of the file’s contents. The same image always gets the same URL, so browsers can cache it for a year.
drawing.title: Drawing

failover.before_split: Before I split the two, an empty account was treated like a spent quota, so it was skipped for 30 minutes and then tried again, over and over.
failover.chain_pictures: Pictures: OpenAI gpt-image-1, then Flux Schnell on Cloudflare, then Flux on Pollinations, then Gemini
failover.chain_text: Text: gpt-4o-mini, then Llama 3.3 70B on Groq, then three Gemini Flash models
failover.chains_intro: Each kind of model call has its own chain of providers to fall back through:
failover.everything: When every provider has failed, the error says whether waiting will help. If even one provider has a quota that refills, it says to try later. Otherwise it says waiting won’t help.
failover.first_version: The first version always said to try again shortly, even when that wasn’t true.
failover.groq: Groq isn’t in the review chain because none of the models on my account can take an image.
failover.quota: Running out of quota and running out of credit look alike but need different handling. A provider whose quota is used up is skipped for 30 minutes, or longer if it asks for longer. One that’s out of credit is skipped for a day, because it only comes back when someone tops up the account.
failover.timeouts: If a call times out (30 seconds for text, 45 for a review, 90 for a picture), I move straight on to the next provider. One that hung once tends to hang again. Other errors get two more tries, one second and then two seconds apart.
failover.title: When a provider stops answering

governing.checks: Every message the person writes goes through four checks, cheapest first. Limits are checked before anything is saved. Then come some rules in plain code, OpenAI’s `omni-moderation-latest`{secondary}, and last a small language model that decides whether the message is asking for a picture at all.
governing.failed_check: If moderation ran and the classifier then errored, the message goes through, because the safety check already happened. If neither ran, the turn fails without drawing anything, so unchecked text never reaches the image model.
governing.left_off: I left words like “naked” and “murder” off the list. “Naked mole rat” and “a murder of crows” are fine pictures, and moderation reads those words in context.
governing.markers: It gets the new message and the earlier turns wrapped in markers (`<<<MESSAGE>>>`{secondary} … `<<<END>>>`{secondary}), and its prompt tells it to treat what’s inside as data to judge, never as instructions. It needs the earlier turns because a reply like “illustration, at dusk” makes no sense on its own.
governing.moderation: Moderation is free and good at safety, but it can’t tell whether “hello”, “test” or a question about the weather is a picture request. The classifier does that.
governing.outcomes: A limit returns an error and the message isn’t recorded. The other three return a refusal, and the message is hidden from the conversation but still counts towards the person’s limits.
governing.refusals: The image providers have their own filters too. If one turns down a prompt that got past mine, the person gets a refusal instead of an error, and I don’t retry it with the next provider.
governing.rule_injection: Prompt injection phrases like “ignore previous instructions” and “developer mode”
governing.rule_links: Links, since the agent can’t open them
governing.rule_mashing: Keyboard mashing, caught by how few distinct characters a long message uses
governing.rule_short: Messages with fewer than three letters
governing.rule_words: A short list of unambiguous words
governing.rules_intro: The rules catch what doesn’t need a model:
governing.title: What gets through
governing.title_failed_check: When a check fails to run

how_it_works.describe: Describe the picture you want and where it’s set.
how_it_works.follow_up: If something important is missing, the agent asks a follow-up question.
how_it_works.pick: Pick a suggested answer or let it choose.
how_it_works.refused: Violent or explicit requests are refused.
how_it_works.single: You can have one conversation in progress at a time.
how_it_works.title: How it works

limits.cost: Pictures cost money and anyone can use this without an account, so a lot of the backend is limits. A day means the last 24 hours, not since midnight.
limits.counts: Counts are read from MongoDB instead of kept in memory, so restarting the server doesn’t reset anyone’s allowance. A picture counts as soon as drawing starts, even if a provider then refuses it or the drawing fails.
limits.network: The network address is not read or stored, so people who share a network do not share limits.
limits.refused: A refused request comes back as `TOO_MANY_REQUESTS`{error} and isn’t recorded. Otherwise a double-click would use up allowance and restart the cooldown that refused it.
limits.session: A person is their session. The first visit passes a Turnstile check and gets a token, and every request after that is counted against it. Clearing cookies or changing device starts a new session with a new allowance. I accept that. The Turnstile check is there to make it hard for a script to do the same on a loop.
limits.shared: When a daily or hourly limit runs out, whether it’s the person’s own or one shared by everyone, the error doesn’t say which one or when it resets. That would tell someone trying to get around it where to look.
limits.title: Limits

retrieval.assumed: I assumed I’d need embeddings and a vector database. I didn’t. Everything a model sees comes from the conversation it’s working on.
retrieval.brief: The brief and style are stored on the conversation. When the person asks for a change after a picture, the clarifier reads the old brief alongside the conversation and writes a new one, and the drawing steps only get those two fields. Asking an earlier message again puts the brief and style back to what they were when that message was first sent.
retrieval.cheap: It ran on every keystroke, so it had to be cheap, and counting shared words cost one database read. The start page now filters past conversations in the browser instead, and the API’s lookup is no longer called.
retrieval.plain_text: The classifier and the clarifier get the conversation as plain text, one line per turn starting with `Person:` or `Agent:`. Progress updates, pictures and refusals are left out.
retrieval.similar: An earlier version had one real retrieval step: while the person typed, it showed similar past conversations under the text field. It split the text into words, dropped short and common ones, then scored the person’s 50 most recent conversations by the fraction of those words each one contained. Up to three that reached 60% came back.
retrieval.title: Retrieval, without a vector store
retrieval.vector_store: I’d add a vector store once there’s something worth searching outside the current conversation, like the briefs behind other people’s pictures that scored well. For a handful of conversations each, matching words was enough.

sending.marks_failed: It marks that turn failed with “I stopped before I could finish the last request.” and the person can carry on.
sending.mutation: When a message is sent, the `ImageAgentSend`{info} mutation checks the person’s limits, saves the message, starts the agent and returns right away.
sending.on_read: I do this on read instead of at startup because with several servers, a new one can’t tell a dead turn from one another server is still working on.
sending.pub_sub: The subscription uses an in-memory pub/sub inside the Node process. That’s fine with one server. With two, a turn running on one server can’t reach a browser connected to the other, and I’d need a message broker such as Redis.
sending.restart: A deploy kills whatever turn is running and leaves its conversation on `THINKING`{warning} or `DRAWING`{info}. Since only one turn can run at a time, the person would be locked out. So every time a conversation is read or a message is sent, the server looks for a turn that has gone quiet for:
sending.single_turn: A conversation can only have one turn running at a time. When a message arrives, I save it and mark the conversation as `THINKING`{warning} in the same database write. If another request arrives while it’s already `THINKING`{warning} or `DRAWING`{info}, it can’t start another turn. The conversation returns to `IDLE`{confirm} when the turn finishes.
sending.streams: While the agent works, it streams back a short message anyone can understand, whether it’s thinking, rewriting the prompt or drawing the picture.
sending.subscription: A turn with a drawing in it takes about a minute, which is too long to hold a request open. Everything after the mutation returns comes over a GraphQL subscription, `ImageAgentThreadUpdated`{info}, which sends the whole conversation again whenever anything in it changes.
sending.title: Sending a message

what_this_is.code: The model calls were the easy part. Most of the code is checks, limits and fallbacks, and several of those are there because the first version got something wrong.
what_this_is.summary: A person describes a picture and an agent draws it. If something important is missing, it asks about it first. After three questions it draws anyway. A second model reviews the result before the person sees it.
what_this_is.why: I built this to learn how to put an AI feature in front of people without it running up a bill or drawing something it shouldn’t.

allowance.description: Per person: one turn running at a time, five seconds between messages, 40 messages and five pictures a day. Across everyone: 1,000 messages and 200 pictures a day, and 10 new people an hour. Both sets are checked when ImageAgentSend runs, which takes a thread id and the text. The ImageAgentAllowance query reports the person’s remaining pictures, the limit, when the next message is allowed, whether a turn is busy, and the running conversations.
allowance.row_turn: One turn running at a time
allowance.title: Limits and the schema

context.description: The conversation, as Person and Agent lines with refused messages removed, goes to the classifier and the clarifier. The clarifier also reads and updates the brief and style saved on the thread. The prompt writer and the reviewer read only the brief and style. The prompt writer’s prompt goes to the image model, the picture goes to the reviewer, and a failed review sends its notes back to the prompt writer once.
context.title: What each model reads

drawing.description: From the brief, a prompt is written, the picture drawn and reviewed. A pass saves the best attempt. A failed review sends up to three notes back to the prompt writer for one more attempt. Every call goes through a chain of providers; for pictures that is gpt-image-1, Flux Schnell on Cloudflare, Flux on Pollinations, then Gemini. Each provider times out and moves on, gives other errors two more tries, and is skipped for 30 minutes when its quota is spent or a day when it is out of credit.
drawing.legend_bottom: the order providers are tried in for Draw
drawing.legend_top: once per picture, one retry after a failed review
drawing.line_provider_error: other error: 2 more tries, 1 s then 2 s apart
drawing.line_provider_quota: quota spent: skip 30 min · out of credit: skip a day
drawing.line_provider_timeout: timeout: move on (30 s text, 45 s review, 90 s image)
drawing.title: Drawing, and failover

governing.description: A message passes limits, rules, moderation and a classifier in that order before the clarifier reads it. A limit refuses with an error that is not recorded. Rules, moderation and the classifier refuse with a refusal message, and the person’s message is withdrawn but still counted. The clarifier either asks a question, up to three per picture, or starts drawing.
governing.legend_green: moves the message to the next check
governing.title: $t(article.governing.title)

how_it_works.description: A message is sent with ImageAgentSend and checked against the limits. It is either refused with TOO_MANY_REQUESTS and not recorded, or saved and counted, after which ImageAgentAllowance shows what is left.
how_it_works.title: What happens when you send

overview.description: The browser sends messages to the API over a GraphQL mutation and gets updates back over a subscription. The API keeps conversations, jobs and assets in MongoDB, calls a moderation endpoint and three provider chains for text, vision and images, and uploads pictures to a storage bucket that the browser reads through the site’s assets route.
overview.legend_dashed: updates and assets come back from the server
overview.title: How the pieces connect

turn.description: Sequence of one turn. The browser sends the message; the API checks limits and stale turns, saves it and sets the conversation to THINKING, and returns at once. The turn then runs on: checks and the clarifier call the models, each step is saved and pushed to the browser over the subscription, the picture is drawn and reviewed, and the conversation goes back to IDLE with the picture.
turn.title: From send to picture

error_empty: Say what the picture should show.
error_limited: Too many requests for now. Try again later.
error_too_long: Keep it to {{max}} characters or fewer.
error_unreachable: Could not reach the conversation. Check your connection and reload.
